title: GS Engineering & Construction turns to modular tech to speed up AI data center builds - mbiz.heraldcorp.com
content: Five companies, including GS Engineering & Construction and LG Uplus, sign MOU Partners to jointly develop hyperscale prefabricated modular data center standard model GS Engineering & Construction announced Monday it will develop a standard model for prefabricated modular data centers, or PMDCs, incorporating modular construction technology to meet surging demand for AI data centers. The company signed a "PMDC Alliance" memorandum of understanding Friday at LG Uplus' Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province. GS Engineering & Construction CEO Heo Yun-hong, LG Uplus CEO Hong Beom-sik, Xi C&A CEO Kim Uk-su, Gansam Architects & Partners CEO Park Mu-chan and D&O CM CEO Lee Yeong-ho attended the signing ceremony. In the AI data center market, the rapid spread of generative AI services and growing demand for GPU-based high-performance computing have made "time to market," or TTM — the ability to deliver infrastructure precisely when customers need it — a key competitive differentiator. The PMDC standard model to be developed under the agreement uses a modular approach in which structural components and major systems such as power and cooling are prefabricated off-site and then assembled on location, optimizing the process for faster construction. Through the partnership, each participating company will draw on its own area of expertise to jointly develop and commercialize a hyperscale PMDC standard model applicable to large-scale AI data centers. GS Engineering & Construction will review the PMDC model's architectural structure, construction methods, schedule-reduction strategies and cost appropriateness. Through the collaboration, the company plans to sharpen its PMDC execution capabilities by applying standardization, modularization and schedule-compression measures from the design stage onward — enabling faster and more flexible responses to customer requirements in future AI data center projects and reinforcing its competitiveness in large-scale data center engineering, procurement and construction. "In the AI data center market, the ability to build a data center reliably and quickly — exactly when customers need it — is becoming a critical competitive edge," a GS Engineering & Construction official said. "Through this PMDC collaboration framework, we will continue to strengthen our competitiveness in building AI data centers optimized for the domestic environment." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction recently reported preliminary second-quarter revenue of 2.78 trillion won ($2.04 billion) and operating profit of 91.4 billion won.

GS Construction to Develop 'Prefabricated Modular' Data Center for Faster Delivery GS Construction is launching the development of a standard model for a Prefabricated Modular Data Center (PMDC) by integrating modular technology, in order to respond quickly to the surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On the 4th, a business agreement was signed to establish PMDC at LG Uplus Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi-do, with Yoon Hong Huh, CEO of GS Construction (second from left), taking a commemorative photo. GS Construction On September 7, GS Construction announced that it had concluded a "business agreement for the establishment of a PMDC alliance" at the LG Uplus Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province. The signing ceremony, held on September 4, was attended by Yoon Hong Huh, CEO of GS Construction; Beom Sik Hong, CEO of LG Uplus; Wook Soo Kim, CEO of Xi C&A; Moo Chan Park, CEO of Gansam Architects & Partners; and Young Ho Lee, CEO of D&O CM, among other officials. The standard model PMDC to be developed through this agreement utilizes a modular approach in which main components such as the building structure, power, and cooling systems are prefabricated and then assembled and installed on-site. Compared to conventional on-site construction of data centers, this method not only shortens construction time and standardizes quality, but also mitigates on-site risks and offers advantages for stepwise expansion in response to increasing demand in the future. Each participating company plans to jointly promote the development and commercialization of a hyperscale PMDC standard model suitable for large-scale AI data centers. GS Construction, leveraging its experience in building large data centers, will review the architectural structure, construction methods, measures to shorten the construction schedule, and cost effectiveness for PMDC models applied to new sites. LG Uplus will propose operational technical requirements and business directions based on its experience in operating data centers and understanding of customer demands. Xi C&A will review PMDC models that utilize existing buildings, leveraging its expertise in data center power, mechanical, and cooling systems. Gansam Architects & Partners will be responsible for the standard design of the data center based on its specialized design capabilities. D&O CM will support the establishment of an effective collaboration system from the standpoint of project scheduling, progress, risk, and business management. GS Construction aims to strengthen its capabilities in executing PMDC projects by applying standardization, modularization, and construction period reduction strategies from the design stage. A representative from GS Construction stated, "Through this PMDC cooperative system, GS Construction will continue to enhance its competitiveness in building AI data centers optimized for the domestic environment by combining our extensive experience in large-scale data center EPC projects with modular technology." © The Asia Business Daily. title: GS Engineering Launches 48-Story Premium Officetel Near Omokgyo Station - 조선일보
content: Mokdong Yunseul Jai offers schools, hospitals, and 100% lottery system for 651 units GS Engineering & Construction has opened a model house for ‘Mokdong Yunseul Jai’ in Mokdong, Yangcheon-gu, Seoul, and will begin accepting subscription applications on the 8th. Mokdong Yunseul Jai is being developed on the former KT site at 924, 924-3, and 5 Mokdong, Yangcheon-gu, spanning three buildings with six underground floors to 48 above-ground floors, and 651 units with exclusive areas ranging from 114 to 203㎡. Unlike typical small-scale officetels, it focuses on medium-to-large-sized units tailored to premium residential demand, attracting attention as a high-end housing product. Its key advantage is a 100% lottery system, allowing anyone aged 19 or older to apply regardless of subscription account ownership, homeownership status, or residence. ◇Proximity to Omokgyo Station, Mokdong School District Mokdong Yunseul Jai offers excellent accessibility to major business districts like Yeouido and Gangnam via the nearby Omokgyo Station on Seoul Subway Line 5. The complex shares the Mokdong school district, with nearby schools including Seojeong Elementary, Mokun Middle, Yangjeong High, and Jinmyeong Girls’ High, and walking distance to entrance exam academies. Shopping and cultural facilities such as Hyundai Department Store, E-Mart, Megabox, and large medical institutions like Ewha Mokdong Hospital are also nearby. The complex is adjacent to green spaces like Omok Park, Anyangcheon Stream, and Mokdong Comprehensive Sports Center. Unit allocations by exclusive area are as follows: 115㎡A (118 units), 114㎡B (208 units), 114㎡C (118 units), 119㎡A (T1) (45 units), 120㎡A (T2) (30 units), 120㎡A (T3) (15 units), 117㎡C (T1) (45 units), 118㎡C (T2) (45 units), 203㎡AD (10 units), 202㎡BD (9 units), and 198㎡CD (8 units). The complex prioritizes medium-to-large units to cater to demand for spacious living areas. The lower exterior features artist Ned Kahn’s installation ‘Yunseul,’ creating a shimmering facade that reflects sunlight and wind. The basement floors (1–3) will house the ‘Concord Club by Joseon,’ a 9,000㎡ membership wellness club operated by Josun Hotels & Resorts, featuring an indoor pool, fitness center, golf practice range, sauna, and membership lounge. On the 47th floor of Building 102, the ‘Club Cloud’ sky community includes a wine reserve (storage and tasting space), cafeteria, party-style guesthouse, and work/meeting areas. ◇Balcony Design for All Units, Deferred Interest Payment System Units feature 4-bay layouts (living room and three bedrooms aligned in the same direction), two- or three-sided balconies for openness, and some are designed as duplexes. Key appliances such as system air conditioners, air purifiers, refrigerators, washer-dryers, dishwashers, induction cooktops, and microwave ovens, along with kitchen furniture and Italian porcelain tiles and ceramic panels, are provided as standard. Fitness facilities will be directly owned and operated by the developer to reduce fixed management fees for residents. A deferred interest payment system applies, and if the loan interest rate exceeds 2.5% annually, the excess interest will be covered by the project operator. A source from GS Engineering & Construction stated, “Mokdong Yunseul Jai combines a prime location near Omokgyo Station with Mokdong’s educational and lifestyle infrastructure, offering differentiated value. We will strive to establish it as a regional landmark that allows residents to enjoy future value from Mokdong’s redevelopment.” The model house is located at 919-8 Mokdong. Applications will be accepted via the Korea Real Estate Board’s subscription platform from the 8th, with winners announced on the 11th and contracts held on the 13th–14th. Move-in is scheduled for the second half of 2030.

title: The Jamaican Riddim Behind Karol G’s Chart-Topping ‘BbY WOW’ - DancehallMag
content: Karol G’s “BbY WOW” is sitting at number one on Spotify’s Global Top 50, Apple Music’s Global 100, and the Billboard Hot Latin chart, racking up over 78 million streams. But the detail that’s got music heads talking isn’t the chart position, it’s the drum pattern that kicks in around 30 seconds into the song. That pattern belongs to “Coolie Dance Riddim,” a dancehall instrumental built by Jamaican producer Cordel Skatta Burrell back in 2003. Burrell originally created it for a wave of dancehall artists, including Sean Paul, Elephant Man, Bounty Killer, and Ce’Cile, who each put their own style over the beat across two compilation albums released that year. The riddim didn’t stay in dancehall for long. By 2004, it was everywhere, powering Nina Sky and Jabba’s “Move Ya Body” and Pitbull and Lil Jon’s “Culo,” which later got a remix with reggaeton veteran Ivy Queen. If you were near a radio or a dancefloor that year, you heard it constantly. The beat kept moving through the decade. Lumidee and Fatman Scoop flipped it in 2006 for “Dance!,” which also pulled in Whitney Houston’s vocals from “I Wanna Dance With Somebody.” Latin artists like Angel y Khriz rode it on their massive hit “Na De Na,” and Jr Ranks added his own take with “Dale Candela.” The riddim had a way of fitting whatever energy an artist brought to it. After going relatively quiet post-2009, “Coolie Dance Riddim” has had a serious revival over the last six years, and this time it’s artists far outside the Caribbean leading the charge. Argentine artist Ms Nina slowed it down for her 2019 album intro, Spanish rapper Cruzzi gave it a lo-fi texture in 2023, and Kehlani used it as the foundation for “After Hours,” the lead single from her 2024 album CRASH. The riddim has also taken off in Turkey in a big way. Sefo and Demet Akalın’s “Yerinde Dur” has cleared 329 million YouTube views, and Lvbel C5’s “DOGUSSTAN BERI HAKLIYIM” has over 140 million Spotify streams. French DJs HUGEL and SOLTO pulled it into their 2025 house track “Jamaican (Bam Bam)” alongside Sister Nancy’s classic song of the same name. The Arab pop scene has picked it up four times in under a year alone. Moroccan artist DYSTINCT used it on “YAMA,” which has over 212 million YouTube views and 73 million Spotify streams. Egyptian legend Amr Diab, Palestinian Jordanian singer Dana Salah, and Palestinian Chilean artist Elyanna have all followed with their own versions. DYSTINCT says he first heard the riddim as a kid in Belgium on “Move Ya Body” and always knew he wanted to use it. “ The riddim is usable in so many different styles,” he said. “Even if you heard the riddim sampled in so many songs, it still sounds cool and fresh every time.” Dana Salah, who worked with producers Michael Brun and Rami Afuni on her version “Wedding Riddim,” says she heard echoes of Arab dabke music the first time she listened to the beat. “It has such a strong identity: joyful, playful, and sensual, but it also leaves enough space for every artist to find their own melody and culture inside it,” she explained. “More than 20 years later, your body still understands that rhythm before your brain does.” Latin music historian Katelina “La Gata” Eccleston ties the resurgence directly to nostalgia, especially for millennials who were around when the riddim first blew up. “Riddim culture thrives in artists displaying individuality and creativity over a common beat,” she said, “so if an artist is able to invoke a sense of nostalgia by showing homage to another song with a bar or adding to the beat with lyrics that complement its soundscape, then I think the task is completed.” Burrell himself says the global reach of his creation is something he never takes for granted. “From its birth, I’ve always felt its commercial viability,” he said. “ However, witnessing its growth on an international scale is an experience I relish every time there’s another global release.” He’s been publicly supporting artists who sample the riddim on his Instagram, and called “BbY WOW” a “child of the 2000s,” saying Karol G “did a great job.” Burrell also spoke to how his Jamaican roots shape everything he makes, even when he’s aiming for something with wider reach. “I’ve always tried not to get stuck in a dancehall-only approach, instead drawing inspiration from global music that I’ve connected with,” he said. “The next step was making it palatable for the world to appreciate.” With Karol G’s version now sitting at the top of global charts and new artists in Turkey, France, and across the Arab world still finding fresh ways into the beat, the list of songs built on “Coolie Dance Riddim” keeps growing. title: LG Uplus Forms Modular Data Center Alliance With GS E&C - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Deal Signed With GS E&C, Xi C&A and Others
Partners to Develop Standard PMDC Model LG Uplus is jointly developing a standard model for prefabricated modular data centers (PMDC) with GS E&C and Xi C&A to meet surging demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. LG Uplus (032640.KS) said on the 6th that it signed a memorandum of understanding to build a PMDC alliance with GS E&C (006360.KS), Xi C&A, Gansam Architects & Partners and D&O CM on the 4th at its Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province. Under the PMDC approach, building structures along with power and cooling equipment are standardized and prefabricated at a factory before being assembled on site. Compared with conventional site-based construction, the method shortens build times and improves quality consistency. Drawing on expertise in design, construction, operations and project management, the alliance members have been jointly working since April to develop a standard model that can be applied to actual AI data center (AIDC) projects. Through the agreement, the partners plan to complete a PMDC model competitive not only in South Korea but globally, and to apply it to actual AIDC construction projects. LG Uplus will define operating standards and technical requirements for PMDC, set business direction and validate the model, based on experience accumulated from building and operating data centers nationwide as well as its AIDC in Paju. GS E&C will provide constructability reviews, process optimization and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) capabilities for newly built PMDC models, drawing on its experience in large-scale data center construction and field execution. Xi C&A will handle the development of a retrofit model that can be applied to existing buildings, along with power and cooling optimization. "We will create a PMDC model with global-level competitiveness and continue strengthening our competitiveness in building next-generation AIDCs," said Hong Beom-shik, chief executive of LG Uplus. title: Fans share their feelings ahead of Karol G’s Sun Bowl Performance - KVIA
content:
EL PASO, Texas (KVIA) - Karol G begins her weekend of performances at the Sun Bowl Saturday as part of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour and fans told ABC-7 why she is one of their favorite artists. The fans came from across the country beginning with Texas's neighboring state New Mexico as fans from Deming, Roswell, and the town of Arrey told ABC-7 they made the trip to come see the Colombian singer. Angelica Castañeda, a fan from Roswell, said she drove her daughters 3 hours so they could see Karol G since they are all fans and for Angelica it helps relieve her stress. "For me, when I hear it, it just kind releases my stress and I just play her music and I feel better," Castañeda said. Another fan from New Mexico, Jaileen Loera from Arrey, said it helps her feel 'heard' through the artist's music. "I feel heard, she does a big confidence boost in latinas, we are overseen I want to say when it comes to showing our feelings," Loera said. "I feel like she made it very big to like, speak about your feelings and it's okay to feel a lot and not be over exaggerating about it you know." Lala Castle, a fan who made the trip to El Paso from Chicago, mentioned something similar when mentioning the emotional response the music brings out of her and specifically mentioning when the music brings up love and men. "She talks about love, she talks about how men actually are, some," Castle said. "She puts you in your feelings, she puts you in your thoughts as well and she also talks good about them to. So it's a little bit of everything." title: LG Uplus Unveils Modular AI Data Center Model to Cut Construction Time - 조선일보
content: Collaborating with GS Engineering & Construction and others, LG Uplus standardizes AI infrastructure with prefabricated modular tech, reducing project timelines LG Uplus is collaborating with industry partners to jointly develop a standardized prefabricated modular data center (PMDC) model incorporating modular technology. The strategy aims to establish a cooperative framework to shorten construction periods and standardize quality for AI data centers (AIDC) in response to the rapidly growing demand for AI infrastructure. LG Uplus announced on September 6 that it signed a business agreement on September 4 with GS Engineering & Construction, Jai C&A, Gansam Architecture, and D&O CM at the Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province, to form a PMDC alliance. The PMDC under development standardizes building structures, power, and cooling facilities, which are prefabricated in factories and assembled on-site using a modular approach. Compared to traditional on-site construction, this method reduces project timelines, ensures quality standardization, and allows flexible infrastructure supply in response to changing demand. With the recent AI boom driving surging demand for data centers, the ability to rapidly supply AI infrastructure has become a key competitive factor in the industry. Consequently, PMDC, which offers supply flexibility and operational efficiency, is gaining attention as a next-generation data center model. The alliance members have jointly pursued standard model development since April, leveraging their respective expertise to apply PMDC to actual AI data center projects. They reviewed a hyperscale PMDC model for large-scale AI data centers consuming 100MW-class power and a retrofit model for converting existing buildings into data centers. Subsequently, they finalized detailed designs and technical specifications tailored to South Korea’s data center environment, along with each company’s roles and business execution framework. LG Uplus will establish operational standards and technical requirements for PMDC based on its experience in constructing and operating nationwide data centers and the Paju AIDC. It will also lead business direction setting and model verification. GS Engineering & Construction will review architectural structures, construction methods, timeline reduction strategies, and cost appropriateness for PMDC models applied to new sites, drawing on its experience in large-scale data center projects. LG Uplus CEO Hong Bum-shik stated, “In the AI era, the core competitive edge for data centers lies in the ability to build necessary infrastructure promptly in line with rapidly changing customer demands. We will strengthen our competitiveness in next-generation AIDC construction by developing a globally competitive PMDC model.”

title: The Short Lived Performance Car That Deserved Better - HotCars
content: Jared has spent 15 years covering the auto industry, getting his first break with autoX—one of Asia’s biggest auto magazines. Since 2010, he has reviewed hundreds of cars and motorbikes around the world, worked with Top Gear, Autocar, Evo, Motoring World, and Quattroruote, served on the IMOTY jury for five years, and is a founding member of the Automotive Journalist Association of India (AJAI). Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update BMW M-Cars wrote the rulebook for the performance sedan. Audi has long been a formidable presence in the segment, and Mercedes perfected the "German muscle car" with their V8-powered AMGs, but credible non-German challengers have always been rare. What makes the landscape even more challenging is that the market has been shifting decisively away from traditional performance vehicles. Sports cars are few and far between, coupes that are not dedicated sports cars are nearly extinct, and SUVs and crossovers have become the default choice for most buyers. The SUV craze began in the late 1990s and early 2000s, with pioneers like the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V anchoring the economy end of the spectrum, while the Mercedes-Benz ML and the Lexus RX300 effectively invented the modern luxury crossover class. With crossovers now the industry standard, performance cars have had to evolve in tandem. You can't build a performance variant of a vehicle you no longer sell — and since automakers are moving crossovers the way McDonald's moves burgers and fries, while sedans are quietly fading like Circuit City and RadioShack, it only makes sense that the ranks of performance sedans and coupes have thinned considerably. There is nothing inherently wrong with something like the X5M, but performance sedans have always held a special appeal for enthusiasts that no SUV has quite managed to replicate. Thankfully, there are still some fantastic performance sedans on the market — but there is one in particular that deserved to stick around a little longer. The muscle car is American, the exotic sports car Italian, and the performance saloon German. Obviously, this is a generalization, but such widely held perceptions of certain market segments have a real impact on how consumers shop. A common critique levied at something like the Genesis G90 is that it isn't quite up to the standard of the S-Class. That isn't entirely untrue, but buyers often begin their evaluation of a Genesis, Acura, Cadillac, or Lexus by assuming it could never surpass a “proper” German luxury sedan. While American, Japanese, and Korean automakers have all built exceptional luxury and performance sedans, overcoming those deeply ingrained perceptions remains an uphill battle. Much like General Motors and John DeLorean inventing the muscle car in 1964, BMW ostensibly invented the modern sports sedan in 1984 with the introduction of the E28 M5. The first-ever M5 was powered by a 3.5L I6 that produced 256 horsepower in the North American market. The iconic E30 M3 arrived just two years later, and two years after that the second-generation M5, the E34, upped displacement to 3.6L (3.8L post-facelift in Europe) and pushed output past 300 horsepower. And if the E34 didn't cement the M5 legacy, the legendary 4.9L V8-powered E39 most certainly did. Mercedes followed suit in 1993 with the first production AMG, the C36. In the years that followed, some incredible cars continued the lineage — the C36 gave way to the V8-powered C43, C55, and C63. The E39 was succeeded by the 5.0L V10-powered E60, and Audi was busy fitting V8s and V10s into its S and RS cars throughout the 2000s. Just as the Mustang defined the pony car, these German sports sedans defined their segment, making it that much harder for outside competitors to carve out a lasting place. Find a car enthusiast and ask them which sports sedan on the current market would be their pick. If you ask me? I'll take a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing, thank you very much. And it's not just because you get a 6.2L supercharged V8 producing 650 horsepower — borrowed from the C7 Z06 — paired with the brilliant MagneRide suspension. No, despite my great appreciation for many automatics, I simply prefer a manual transmission. I'm certainly not in the minority, and aside from the M3, Cadillac is the only other game in town when it comes to rowing your own gears in a four-door sedan. No manual has been offered in the M5 since the F10 generation, and no manual has appeared in an Audi sports sedan since the B8.5 S4 — or the B7 RS4 if you want the full-fat performance model. Cadillac, meanwhile, offers both the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing with 6-speed manuals. The CT5-V Blackwing is the spiritual heir to the original V-car, the CTS-V. When it arrived in 2004 with the 405-horsepower LS6 V8 borrowed from the C5 Corvette Z06, it was the last thing anyone expected from Cadillac. At the time, the brand was riding high on the second-generation Escalade and still selling the DeVille and Seville. There was already plenty of surprise in 2003 when the CTS 3.6L became the first Cadillac offered with a manual transmission since the 1988 Cimarron — nobody was expecting the original CTS-V on top of that, let alone a second generation that paired a manual transmission with 556 supercharged horsepower from the LSA V8. We're quite lucky the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing models have carried that torch, because the Pontiac GXP and Chevy SS came and went faster than the Honda Prologue. The Cadillac offerings have been among the absolute best in this segment for the better part of two decades. The CTS-V and ATS-V — and their successors, the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing — are arguably even better than their respective M5 and M3 counterparts, proving that American brands have a legitimate claim in this space. Japanese and Korean brands have made attempts, but have struggled to establish a long-term foothold. Aside from Lexus, Infiniti and Genesis are the only two of the bunch to have offered a V8, but the M56/Q70 5.6L and G80 5.0L fall well short of true sports sedan status. The Kia Stinger GT2, Genesis G70 3.3T, Infiniti Q50 Red Sport, and Acura TLX Type S are all fantastic cars, but they compete more directly with cars like the S4, M340i, C43 AMG, and the CT4-V (non-Blackwing) than with M Division, AMG, or Blackwing at the top. Lexus is really the only one of the bunch to have genuinely gone after BMW — first with the IS-F, and then with one of the all-time great performance sedans. The GS-F was based on the fourth-generation Lexus GS, introduced in 2011. Unlike the previous generation of GS, which offered V8 trims such as the GS 400, 430, and 460, the final iteration of the Lexus GS was V6-only. It was an excellent V6 — the 3.5L 2GR-FE/FKS — but it didn't quite pack the punch of the V8 cars. That's fine, though, because for the final generation Lexus saved the V8 for something more special: the GS-F. While the previous V8 trims were essentially engine upgrades, the GS-F was a proper sports sedan. It was Lexus's second entry into that market, following the 2008–2014 IS-F. It used the same 8-speed automatic and 5.0L V8 as the IS-F, but produced 51 more horsepower than its predecessor. And as noted, the GS-F is far more than just an engine. Starting in 2017, models received adaptive variable suspension (AVS), which allows the car to adjust the dampers independently across 30 different settings based on driver input, selected mode, and real-time sensor data. All GS-F models also received a torque-vectoring differential that can be set to standard, slalom, or track mode. This is not to be confused with brake torque vectoring, as found on a Fiesta ST — this is a proper mechanical trick diff that automotive journalists consistently praised for allowing this large sedan to rotate through corners like a much smaller machine. The GS-F was also fitted with Brembo 6-piston front and 4-piston rear brakes, giving the driver genuine confidence when scrubbing off speed. The GS-F shares the same wonderful powertrain as the IS-F and RC-F, using the same Aisin AA80E 8-speed automatic — though the GS-F has a shorter final drive ratio than the IS-F and RC-F — and the 2UR-GSE 5.0L V8. Which is to say, it works. The AA80E, which debuted in the 2007 LS 460 as the world's first production 8-speed automatic, has earned an excellent long-term reputation. It most recently appeared in the IS 500 F Sport Performance, which shares the same mechanical core as the proper F models. Both the 2UR-GSE and the Aisin 8-speed are genuinely reliable units. In fact, the entire car is, which is why these have held 60%–70% of their value since new. According to classic.com and comparable sales from major auction sites, the GS-F is currently valued at nearly double that of an equivalent M5 from the same era, despite the performance gap. It's true that contemporary rivals — the aforementioned M5, CTS-V, E63, and RS7 — all made more power and could outpace the GS-F's already brisk 4.4-second sprint to 60 mph. That was a legitimate critique when the car was new, but 467 horsepower and 389 lb-ft of torque are not small numbers. We've been desensitized to power figures that include a comma, but a 193-inch, 4,100-pound sedan reaching 60 mph in the same time as a 981 Cayman S is genuinely impressive. And besides — are you really taking this to the track? Are you racing for pinks? The GS-F may not have been the outright performance king of its era, but given its reliability and its glorious engine note, it deserved another chance. It only lasted five model years, after all. Sadly, though it's possible Toyota could one day fit the 4.0L twin-turbo V8 from the GR GT3 into a new Lexus sports sedan, the sedan market may not survive long enough for that to happen. Lexus currently only offers the front-wheel-drive ES in the sedan segment. Thankfully, the GS-F appears reliable enough to last for decades — just don't expect prices to fall; the market has already figured out how special these cars are. It's just a shame there won't be another. Luxury performance sedans are notorious for shedding value once they leave the showroom. The Lexus GS F hasn't escaped depreciation entirely, but it has aged far more gracefully on the used market than its German rivals. With an original MSRP ranging from about $84,440 for 2016 models to more than $90,000 for a well-optioned 2020 example, the GS F has become more attainable over time, yet it remains remarkably resistant to the steep value drops that typically define this segment. Today, early 2016–2017 cars typically trade anywhere from the high-$30,000s to around $50,000, depending on mileage and condition, while facelifted 2018–2020 examples — which received updated styling and additional standard technology — regularly command well over $50,000. Exceptional low-mileage cars can fetch considerably more, as demonstrated by a 20,000-mile 2020 GS F that sold for $73,500 on Bring a Trailer in early 2025. Meanwhile, buyers can still pick up an F10 BMW M5 for less than $30,000, and even the rare S212 Mercedes-Benz E 63 AMG often changes hands for under $40,000. The contrast highlights just how well the GS F has protected its value. Lexus' hard-earned reputation for reliability is undoubtedly part of the equation, but it's far from the only reason. Lexus' reputation for bulletproof reliability is certainly part of the reason the GS F has depreciated far less than its European rivals, but it's far from the whole story. There are other reasons, starting with sheer rarity. The collector market tends to reward cars that combine genuine performance with genuine scarcity, and the Lexus GS F checks both boxes. While BMW and Mercedes-AMG built their M5 and E63 in far greater numbers, Lexus produced roughly 4,823 GS Fs worldwide during the model's five-year run, with only about 2,347 examples reaching U.S. buyers. Special editions and uncommon specifications only amplify that exclusivity — the 2019 10th Anniversary Edition was capped at 100 U.S. cars, while rare finishes such as Flare Yellow and Molten Pearl have become especially sought-after among enthusiasts. Just as important is what's under the hood. The GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8 belongs to a rapidly shrinking breed of naturally aspirated performance engines, particularly in the sports sedan world. It rewards drivers with immediate throttle response, a broad and predictable power curve, a 7,300-rpm redline, and an exhaust note that no turbocharged engine can quite replicate. Those qualities are even more compelling today, given that there is no naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan currently on sale. After spending so much time praising the GS F, it's fair to ask why Lexus discontinued it after the 2020 model year. The answer has less to do with the GS F itself and more to do with the fate of the GS sedan it was built upon. By the end of its run, the GS had become financially unsustainable. Lexus sold just 3,378 GSs in the U.S. during 2019, accounting for only 4% of the brand's passenger-car sales and less than 1% of the midsize luxury sedan segment. The GS was also squeezed from both sides. Buyers seeking comfort overwhelmingly chose the less expensive ES, while those wanting practicality flocked to the RX, which routinely sold well into six figures annually. With engineering resources increasingly directed toward crossovers, the aging fourth-generation GS received only incremental updates, leaving its interior technology and overall package trailing newer European competitors. As impressive as the GS F was, it couldn't reverse those trends. Against 600-plus-horsepower twin-turbo rivals like the BMW M5 and Mercedes-AMG E 63, its 467-horsepower naturally aspirated V8 appealed to a niche audience. Combined with Lexus' smaller performance-brand footprint, the GS F simply wasn't enough to save the GS nameplate. The GS F belongs to a category that has effectively disappeared. You can no longer walk into a dealership and buy a naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan. Nearly every manufacturer has downsized to turbocharged six-cylinder engines or electrified powertrains in pursuit of stricter emissions targets and improved fuel economy. Even the remaining V8-powered performance sedans rely almost exclusively on forced induction to achieve their staggering power figures. They are undeniably quicker, but they lack the immediate throttle response, progressive power delivery, and intoxicating high-revving character that defined the GS F. To its credit, Lexus kept that philosophy alive a little longer with the IS 500 F SPORT Performance. Sharing the GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8, the smaller sedan produced a slightly improved 472 horsepower and wrapped it in a lighter, more agile package that many enthusiasts considered the spiritual successor to the GS F. The IS 500 F SPORT Performance demonstrated that Lexus still believed there was an audience for a naturally aspirated V8 luxury sports sedan, but it ultimately proved not large enough to overcome market realities.     Production ended after the 2025 model year, bringing Lexus' naturally aspirated V8 sedan lineage to a close. As emission regulations tighten and electrification accelerates, cars like the GS F are becoming relics of a different era. Enthusiasts continue to ask for naturally aspirated V8 sports sedans, but the industry is moving in a different direction. That only makes the GS F more desirable today — not just as a great driver's car, but as a reminder of a performance philosophy that may never return. title: Gen.G's Late-Game Focus Earns 2-1 Match Point - Inven Global
content: Gen.G won Game 3 following Game 2 to take a 2-1 lead. Now just one win away, Gen.G is on the verge of becoming the first team to reach the Grand Finals. In Game 3, both teams focused on farming rather than active skirmishing for the first 10 minutes. Hanwha Life Esports made the first move, committing multiple players to the top lane to take down Kiin's Gwen for first blood. Shortly after, Gen.G retaliated by investing heavily top to kill Zeus's Camille. With an extra kill and a slight edge in macro play, Hanwha Life Esports was unwilling to yield the next Dragon to Gen.G. Despite Hanwha Life holding the gold lead, Gen.G won the teamfight behind Chovy's aggro juggling on Akali, securing their third Dragon stack. content: Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) has emerged as an unexpected winner from the New York Knicks' 2026 NBA championship, although the benefit remains unclear. Players, managers and team employees reportedly received more than $9 billion in bonuses and compensation following the Knicks' first championship since 1973. Star players captured the largest share, creating a wealth-management opportunity for advisers serving the roster. Goldman's wealth management unit reportedly counts several Knicks players as clients, but the bank has not identified them or disclosed how much compensation will enter managed accounts. Investors should view the reported windfall as a potential client inflow rather than a confirmed earnings increase. The connection highlights Goldman's strategy. The bank manages more than $4 trillion across public and private markets and has prioritized wealth management alongside trading and capital markets. Fee-generating assets can provide recurring revenue, offsetting volatility in dealmaking and trading. Professional athletes fit that strategy. Careers can be short, with income concentrated across few years. Goldman has said athlete clients maintain long investment horizons and accept diverse asset mixes. Many also seek stakes in businesses and franchises capable of generating dependable retirement income. The championship could deepen relationships, attract player referrals and add investable assets. Yet the economic impact depends on how much money Goldman captures, which products clients select and the fees involved. Without disclosures, the championship is better viewed as a wealth-gathering opportunity than a material earnings catalyst. Goldman stock gained 0.25% as the report attracted attention. Wall Street remains cautiously positive. Fifteen analysts give GS a Moderate Buy rating, based on six Buys, eight Holds and one Sell. Their average $1,157.79 target implies 8% upside. title: Could the right-wing extremist AfD govern a German state for the first time? - Brookings
content:
Democracy, Conflict, & Governance Foreign Politics & Elections On September 6, the 2.1 million citizens of the small eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt could set off a political earthquake with reverberations all the way to Berlin if, as current polls predict, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) wins the statewide election. An assessment by Germany’s domestic intelligence service that the national AfD is “confirmed right-wing extremist” is currently under judicial review, but a Saxony-Anhalt intelligence report says the classification of the party’s state chapter as confirmed extremist is final. “Its leaders,” asserts the document, have made numerous “Islamophobic, racist, and antisemitic statements,” and it adds that the state party “wants to abolish representative democracy in its current state.” For the tens of millions of Germans for whom citizenship is indivisible from accepting responsibility for the mass atrocities perpetrated by their country under National Socialist rule, this is an appalling prospect. It is no less concerning for many of their European neighbors. The AfD is currently polling at around 41% in Saxony-Anhalt. An absolute majority of votes, and thus the position of minister-president for its top candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is within reach. The runners-up, the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Left Party (the far-left successor to the former East German communist party), are far behind at 23% and 11.5%. But whether the AfD can govern alone will hinge on the performance of smaller parties, whose parliamentary seats will be redistributed if they fail to surmount the 5% threshold: the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), at 8.5%; the Greens, at 6%; the far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), at 4%; and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), at 3%. Indeed, some national initiatives are encouraging Saxony-Anhalt’s voters to cast their ballots tactically for these parties to keep the AfD out of government. (The academic vote simulator Projekt Zweitstimme has the probability of an AfD-only government at 33%.) Should the AfD fail to achieve an outright majority, the task of organizing a CDU-led governing majority faces almost insurmountable difficulties. All the other parties—except BSW, whose leader has offered to play kingmaker for an AfD-led government—maintain a “firewall,” or “Brandmauer,” against any form of cooperation with the AfD. (The ban is functionally moot in many municipalities and districts.) The CDU has tied its hands even more by also excluding any coalition with the Left Party. The clock will be ticking, as state law dictates that a new legislature must be constituted within 30 days of the election. Even if the CDU, which has headed several coalition governments in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 24 years, manages to pull together a coalition or rally the votes for a minority government led by incumbent Minister-President Sven Schulze—whether by relying on votes from the Left Party or poaching AfD state parliamentarians—stable, productive government will likely remain elusive. Profound disagreements on policy issues would guarantee severe tensions in such a cooperation. The state AfD leadership projects optimism that it will govern Saxony-Anhalt. The 35-year-old Siegmund, a glib salesman with a degree in business psychology who once cofounded a company for room fragrances, has run a remarkably successful campaign. He has built it on discipline, personal charm, and friendly evasiveness when prodded on policy questions. His chief ideologue and deputy Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is rather less polished. After he tried to quash a video clip that showed a Russian army mug in his office, more clips and posts surfaced: other Russian memorabilia, Tillschneider waving a Russian flag, Tillschneider yelling “our enemies don’t sit in Moscow, they sit in Magdeburg and Berlin!” Both Siegmund and Tillschneider have refused to disavow the AfD’s links to extremist movements like the Identitarian Movement (Identitäre Bewegung) or the Saxon Separatists (Sächsische Separatisten). Some of their own staffers once belonged to a neo-Nazi group. “Sieg! Mund!” is a frequent refrain at AfD rallies across Saxony-Anhalt (Siegmund, for his part, claims to hear no resemblance to a certain historical slogan). When an AfD member of the European Parliament chased down and beat a 14-year-old boy who had sabotaged a campaign poster in August with a baseball bat, neither Siegmund nor the state AfD condemned the act. Siegmund’s pitch to voters is that the AfD will restore the country to “Germany, but normal.” Yet his party’s ideas about governance are anything but. The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt chapter published a stunningly radical 258-page “government program” in March, which The New York Times called “partly unworkable, far exceeding the power of a state government.” Many of its proposals would be familiar to MAGA voters: segregation or deportation of refugees, abolition of funding for public broadcasters, total overhaul of schools and law enforcement, no more wind farms, rollback of LGBTQ+ rights, rejection of historical guilt, overtures to Russia. It condemns the Bauhaus school of design—whose roots in Saxony-Anhalt trace back to the 1920s—in coded language reminiscent of Nazi-era attacks on “rootless cosmopolitans.” The Halle Institute for Economic Research says that implementing the AfD party platform would cost 2.2 billion euros (about $2.5 billion) in excess of what the state budget provides annually. Legal experts writing on the Verfassungsblog platform have argued that some of the program’s key components, such as its chapter on migration, would be unconstitutional. Insiders have raised doubts that an AfD government could fill the 150 to 200 state leadership positions necessary to govern, despite the creation of a training school for AfD cadres in 2025. Why the AfD—one of Europe’s most blatantly far-right parties, which is openly bent on changing the country’s constitutional order and has zero experience in democratic governance—has such appeal is a subject of intense debate in Germany. It is the largest opposition party in the national legislature and leads the polls nationwide at 29%. Its support is strongest in the former East Germany, but its origins are in the western states, where its appeal is growing. And while it was long considered a protest party, ideological conviction increasingly drives its voters. Analysts point to a range of factors: former Chancellor Angela Merkel’s “triangulation” and liberalization of the CDU, which left the right uncovered; economic inequality, weak civic infrastructure, and declining party identification; and resentment of what some critics call West Germany’s “colonization” of the former East after reunification in 1990. Ulrich Siegmund himself—in a calculated appeal to Ostalgie (nostalgia for preunification East Germany)—is promising voters that an AfD government will bring back “our good old, safe Germany.” Numerous interviewers have asked him how this vision comports with Soviet occupation, the cruelty of the Communist Stasi police, or the rise of neo-Nazi skinheads who terrorized rural villages after the fall of the Berlin Wall, often armed with baseball bats (Baseballschlägerjahre), to no avail. Another area of fierce contention is what could be done to defend the state’s democratic institutions against unconstitutional attack. Central to Germany’s constitution (the Basic Law) is the principle of militant democracy: the constitutional order must not remain neutral when faced with forces trying to abolish it. A much-discussed possible safeguard provided for by the Basic Law would be an outright party ban, but the political and legal hurdles are extremely high. There are also only two cases of a successful ban in postwar German history, both in the 1950s. Lawyers and practitioners across the country have been wargaming other ways to safeguard institutions and democratic processes in the case of the AfD gaining a foot in the door of power—or an AfD-run state attempting to block the passage of NATO troops moving to Europe’s eastern flank in case of a security contingency. There are two further state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin on September 20, where the AfD polls at 37% and 18%, respectively; it has little to no chance of gaining power in either. But if support for the CDU and SPD—who form the governing coalition in Berlin led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz—erodes in all three states, that could have national consequences. Calls abound within the SPD for cochairs Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas, both of whom hold cabinet positions, to relinquish the party leadership in this case. There have also been speculations within the CDU that Merz’s chancellorship might come into jeopardy. The chancellor—who once promised to cut AfD support in half but instead has seen it double—is consistently unpopular; so much so that his eastern German peers, including Schulze in Saxony-Anhalt, are keeping him at arm’s length. Meanwhile, the national AfD leadership is reveling in its prospects. Cochair Alice Weidel said in a prime-time television interview that her party seeks to rule the entire country, and that Saxony-Anhalt is “only the beginning.” Indeed, the AfD is looking at a win-win—whether it cuts its teeth on state-level governance now and uses Saxony-Anhalt as a laboratory for radical change in the rest of the country, or whether it further twists the knife on establishment parties forced into unwieldy, ideologically disparate coalitions to keep it from power. Either outcome is likely to make Germany more introverted and less capable of decisive political action, at a time when its neighbors in Europe need it to be exactly the opposite.
